explanations.explanation: That's the order, baker. Joseph, Jacob's son and second only to Pharaoh in Egypt, directs the physicians in his service to embalm his father, and they do it (Genesis 50:2). He doesn't hand the job to just anyone. He gives it to the people who work for him. I like that he stays close to this one himself.

I see why spices came to mind, because the verse is about care and preparation. But the text names a different job. Joseph directs the physicians to embalm his father Israel, and they embalm him (Genesis 50:2). Nothing in the verse mentions burning. Joseph, Jacob's son, is giving a careful order here.

A same-day burial would be quick, but that's not how this goes. Joseph gives the order to embalm his father, and the next verse says it takes forty days to complete (Genesis 50:2-3). Then the Egyptians mourn seventy days. Friend, this is a slow, careful goodbye. Nobody here is rushing it, and I wouldn't either.

True. The verse says, “And the Egyptians mourned for him seventy days.” (Genesis 50:3). That's a whole country grieving alongside Joseph's family. Seventy days is a long time to keep the mourning going, and nobody cuts it short.

The verse actually says the opposite, baker. “And the Egyptians mourned for him seventy days.” (Genesis 50:3). So it's true that they mourn for Jacob, Joseph's father, and they do it for seventy days. That's a long stretch, and I think it says something about how much Joseph's father mattered there.

explanations.answer: Bury him in the land of Canaan
explanations.explanation: Yes, and Joseph quotes his father word for word to Pharaoh, Egypt's king. “You must bury me in the tomb that I dug for myself in the land of Canaan.” (Genesis 50:5). Jacob dug that tomb himself, so it was no random spot. Joseph treats the oath like the serious promise it is.

explanations.answer: Stay in the land of Egypt
explanations.explanation: Jacob did come down to Egypt, so I get the mix-up. But the oath points the other way. Joseph tells Pharaoh his father said, “You must bury me in the tomb that I dug for myself in the land of Canaan.” (Genesis 50:5). The oath is about going back to Canaan, not staying put.

Pharaoh's tomb never comes up, baker. Joseph says his father made him swear to bury him in “the tomb that I dug for myself in the land of Canaan.” (Genesis 50:5). Jacob had his own tomb picked out and dug. That's where Joseph is aiming, and Egypt isn't on the map for it.

True. Joseph asks, “Now let me go and bury my father, and then return.” (Genesis 50:5). He tells Pharaoh up front that he's coming back. That's a man who wants the whole plan on the table before he asks for anything.

The message says otherwise, friend. Joseph asks, “Now let me go and bury my father, and then return.” (Genesis 50:5). So he promises to come back to Egypt once the burial is done. He asks for the trip and tells Pharaoh the trip has an end.

explanations.answer: Go up and bury your father
explanations.explanation: That's it. Pharaoh answers, “Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear to do.” (Genesis 50:6). That's a quick, clear yes, and it points right back to the oath. Joseph asked carefully and got a plain answer.

explanations.answer: Send your brothers in your place
explanations.explanation: Pharaoh doesn't offer a substitute. He tells Joseph himself, “Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear to do.” (Genesis 50:6). The very next verse has Joseph going (Genesis 50:7). The brothers go along, but nobody is sent instead of him.

explanations.answer: Stay and bury him here in Egypt
explanations.explanation: That would've sent Joseph in the opposite direction. Pharaoh actually says, “Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear to do.” (Genesis 50:6). Joseph is allowed to keep the oath he swore. Pharaoh doesn't argue with it at all.

The brothers don't stay behind, baker. The text says Joseph goes up with his household, “and his brothers, and his father’s household.” (Genesis 50:8). Only the children and the flocks and herds are left in Goshen. Everybody old enough to travel is on that road.

False is right, and you can count heads to see it. Joseph goes “along with all of Joseph’s household, and his brothers, and his father’s household.” (Genesis 50:8). Only their children and flocks and herds stay in Goshen. It's the biggest family trip I've ever heard of, and I once crowded six cookie cutters onto one counter.

Yes, and nobody is holding back. At the threshing floor of Atad, “they lamented and wailed loudly, and Joseph mourned for his father seven days.” (Genesis 50:10). That's a big crowd with big grief. It's loud enough that the people living nearby notice, as the next verse shows.

It's quite the opposite, friend. The verse says they “lamented and wailed loudly” (Genesis 50:10). The Canaanites living there hear and see it too, and they comment on it (Genesis 50:11). Silence wouldn't have drawn a single comment.

No songs here, baker. The text says they “lamented and wailed loudly,” and Joseph mourned for his father seven days (Genesis 50:10). This is a time of grief, plain and open. I think it's good that the text lets them mourn out loud.

That's what they say. The Canaanites see the mourning and declare, “This is a solemn ceremony of mourning by the Egyptians.” (Genesis 50:11). With that many chariots and Egyptian elders in the crowd, I can see how they'd say it. That's why the place across the Jordan got its name, Abel-mizraim.

Hittites do show up in this passage, but not here. The Canaanites say, “This is a solemn ceremony of mourning by the Egyptians.” (Genesis 50:11). Ephron the Hittite shows up a few verses later as the man Abraham bought the burial field from (Genesis 50:13). That's a different moment from this one.

The Amorites aren't mentioned in this passage at all, baker. What the Canaanites say is, “This is a solemn ceremony of mourning by the Egyptians.” (Genesis 50:11). They're looking at the crowd that came up from Egypt and putting a name on it. The name they land on is the Egyptians.

That's the place. Jacob's sons buried him “in the cave at Machpelah in the field near Mamre” (Genesis 50:13). Abraham bought that field from Ephron the Hittite to use as a burial site. Joseph kept his oath, and the sons did as their father had charged them (Genesis 50:12).

Bethlehem is a real place, but it isn't named here. The verse says they buried him “in the cave at Machpelah in the field near Mamre” (Genesis 50:13). It's the field Abraham had bought as a burial site. I mix up my cookie tins all the time too, friend, so no worries.

Shechem doesn't come up in this passage. The text says Jacob's sons buried him “in the cave at Machpelah in the field near Mamre” (Genesis 50:13). That's the field Abraham purchased from Ephron the Hittite. Machpelah is the name to hold onto.

explanations.answer: Repay them for the evil they did
explanations.explanation: That's their fear, plain and simple. They say, “What if Joseph bears a grudge? Then he will surely repay us for all the evil that we did to him.” (Genesis 50:15). Their father is gone, and they start imagining the worst. I think a guilty conscience can talk louder than anybody in the room.

explanations.answer: Send them all back to Canaan
explanations.explanation: Canaan never comes up in what they fear. They say, “What if Joseph bears a grudge? Then he will surely repay us for all the evil that we did to him.” (Genesis 50:15). Their worry is about payback for what they did to him. That's a heavier fear than a move.

Nothing about flocks in their words, baker. They say, “What if Joseph bears a grudge? Then he will surely repay us for all the evil that we did to him.” (Genesis 50:15). The fear is about what they did to Joseph and what he might do back. The flocks aren't part of it.

That's the word. The brothers say their father commanded, “I beg you, please forgive the transgression and sin of your brothers, for they did you wrong.” (Genesis 50:17). That's an honest thing to say out loud. They name the wrong and ask for forgiveness anyway.

Nobody's asking for a prize here, friend. The brothers say their father commanded, “I beg you, please forgive the transgression and sin of your brothers, for they did you wrong.” (Genesis 50:17). What they want is forgiveness. A reward would be a very different conversation.

Blessing is close to the mood, but it isn't the word in the verse. The brothers say their father commanded, “I beg you, please forgive the transgression and sin of your brothers, for they did you wrong.” (Genesis 50:17). They're asking Joseph to forgive. They know exactly what they did.

Joseph doesn't get angry, baker. The verse says, “When their message came to him, Joseph wept.” (Genesis 50:17). I think this one hurts, because it's tears and not a temper that answer the message. The text gives us weeping, and that's what he does.
False is right. “When their message came to him, Joseph wept.” (Genesis 50:17). The text shows tears and no anger. After that, the brothers come to him themselves (Genesis 50:18).
They go all the way down. The brothers come, bow down before Joseph, and say, “We are your slaves!” (Genesis 50:18). They don't hold anything back. It's a big thing to say to your own brother.

No soldiers in this scene, friend. The brothers bow down before Joseph and say, “We are your slaves!” (Genesis 50:18). That's about as low as a person can put themselves. Soldiers would at least be standing.

Judges would be sitting above Joseph, and they're doing the opposite. They bow down and say, “We are your slaves!” (Genesis 50:18). Joseph even answers that he isn't in the place of God (Genesis 50:19). So he's not taking a judge's seat either.
That's his first word to them. Joseph says, “Do not be afraid.” (Genesis 50:19). The brothers walked in scared, bowing low, and that's the first thing they hear. It's a kind way to start.

Joseph never sends them away. The first thing he says is, “Do not be afraid.” (Genesis 50:19). Later he even promises, “I will provide for you and your little ones.” (Genesis 50:21). So leaving isn't on his mind.
Joseph doesn't ask for proof in this passage, baker. His first words to them are, “Do not be afraid.” (Genesis 50:19). They come to him bowing low and afraid. What they get first is comfort.

Good is the word. Joseph says, “…what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good…” (Genesis 50:20). He doesn't pretend the evil didn't happen. He says God was working for good through it.

Revenge is the very thing the brothers were afraid of, but Joseph says something else. He first asks, “Am I in the place of God?” (Genesis 50:19). Then he says God intended it “for good” (Genesis 50:20). Payback isn't what he's after.

Ruin is what the brothers feared, baker, but it isn't what Joseph says. He tells them, “…what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good…” (Genesis 50:20). That one word turns the whole sentence around. The evil was theirs, and the good was God's.

explanations.answer: Preserve the lives of many people
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Joseph gives. God intended it “to preserve the lives of many people.” (Genesis 50:20). Joseph names the whole point of the story in one line, and it isn't about him at all. It's about the lives that were kept safe.

explanations.answer: Make Joseph great in all Egypt
explanations.explanation: Joseph doesn't make it about himself. He says God intended it “to preserve the lives of many people.” (Genesis 50:20). His own greatness isn't what he points to. I think that's a humble way to see your own story.
That isn't what Joseph says. He says it was “to preserve the lives of many people.” (Genesis 50:20). Nothing in the verse mentions bringing Pharaoh's people anywhere. The point is lives kept safe.

True, and he says it plainly. Joseph tells them, “I will provide for you and your little ones.” (Genesis 50:21). The brothers came expecting trouble. What they get is a promise to look after them and their families.

The verse says the opposite, baker. Joseph tells them, “I will provide for you and your little ones.” (Genesis 50:21). So it's true that he promises to provide for them and their children. The text adds that he reassured them and spoke kindly.

True. The verse says, “He saw Ephraim’s sons to the third generation…” (Genesis 50:23). Ephraim is Joseph's son (Genesis 41:52). Joseph lives long enough to see great-grandchildren, and that's a full house.

The text says Joseph does see it. “He saw Ephraim’s sons to the third generation…” (Genesis 50:23). Ephraim is Joseph's son (Genesis 41:52). So he lives long enough to see the generations after him grow up.

explanations.answer: Bring them up to the land He promised
explanations.explanation: That's his word of hope. Joseph tells his brothers, “…God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land to the land He promised on oath…” (Genesis 50:24). He's about to die, and he's still looking ahead. He trusts what God said He'd do.

explanations.answer: Make them rulers over all Egypt
explanations.explanation: Joseph says nothing about ruling Egypt. He says, “…God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land…” (Genesis 50:24). The promise points out of Egypt and toward the land God promised. Ruling is a different story.

explanations.answer: Keep them in Goshen for good
explanations.explanation: Goshen isn't where Joseph points them, baker. He says God “will surely visit you and bring you up from this land” (Genesis 50:24). That's a promise about leaving Egypt for the land God promised. Staying forever doesn't fit it.

explanations.answer: Carry his bones up from Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's the oath. Joseph says, “God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones up from this place.” (Genesis 50:25). He wants his bones to go with them when God brings them up. Joseph trusted that day would come.

explanations.answer: Build him a tomb in Egypt
explanations.explanation: No tomb is requested. Joseph says, “…and then you must carry my bones up from this place.” (Genesis 50:25). He's asking to be carried out of Egypt when God attends to them. The oath points forward.

A city isn't what Joseph asks for, friend. He makes them swear, “…and then you must carry my bones up from this place.” (Genesis 50:25). It's a simple request, and he trusts them to keep it. I like a plain ask.

Not yet, baker. The text says Joseph died at 110, and they embalmed his body and placed it in a coffin in Egypt (Genesis 50:26). The carrying up was for later, when God attends to them, as the oath said (Genesis 50:25). I think this part is a quiet, heavy one.

False is right. Joseph died at 110, and they embalmed his body and placed it in a coffin in Egypt (Genesis 50:26). The oath said his bones would be carried up after God attends to them (Genesis 50:25). I think this is a quiet moment, and it's fine to let it be.
